notes.front: What is batch processing?
notes.back: Collecting and storing incoming data records, then processing the whole group together in a single operation.
notes.explanation: When each group runs can be set by a schedule, by the amount of data that has arrived, or by some other event.
notes.example: Like a school office that collects the day’s dinner-money envelopes and counts them all together after the last lesson, rather than as each one arrives.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand batch processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is stream processing?
notes.back: Constantly monitoring a data source and processing each new data event in real time, as it arrives.
notes.explanation: Unlike batch processing, there is no wait for the next batch interval; data is handled as individual units.
notes.example: Like a ticket barrier that counts each passenger as they walk through, rather than counting the crowd at the end of the day.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the lambda architecture?
notes.back: A common pattern for combining batch processing and stream processing in a large-scale data analytics solution.
notes.explanation: Streaming data is captured in real time while data from other sources is batch processed, so both real-time and historical analysis are possible.
notes.example: Like a newsroom that posts live updates as a story breaks and also prints a considered weekly round-up drawing on the same reporting.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Combine batch and stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the kappa architecture?
notes.back: A simpler alternative to lambda that removes the separate batch layer and treats all data as a continuous stream.
notes.explanation: When historical data has to be reprocessed, the stream is replayed instead of being run through a batch layer.
notes.example: Like keeping one recording of a match and rewinding it whenever you need to re-analyse it, instead of also keeping separate written match reports.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Combine batch and stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In stream processing, what is a perpetual query?
notes.back: A query that keeps running over event data as it arrives, selecting, projecting or aggregating it.
notes.explanation: In the general stream processing architecture, event data is often processed by such a query.
notes.example: Like a standing order at a newsagent: set up once, it keeps acting on every new issue without being asked again.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “A general architecture for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In stream processing, what is a temporal window?
notes.back: A time-based period over which streaming data is aggregated, such as counting sensor readings per minute.
notes.explanation: Stream processing typically sees only the most recent data, or the data inside a rolling window such as the last 30 seconds.
notes.example: Like a car park sign that reports how many cars entered in each fifteen-minute slot, not since the car park opened.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “A general architecture for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In stream processing, what is a sink?
notes.back: The output that processing results are written to, such as a file, a database table, a live dashboard or another queue.
notes.explanation: It is the final stage of the general stream processing architecture.
notes.example: Like the tray at the end of a letter-sorting machine where the sorted post lands, ready for the next stage.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “A general architecture for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Apache Kafka?
notes.back: An open-source data ingestion solution commonly used together with Apache Spark.
notes.explanation: The training lists it among the services commonly used to ingest data for stream processing.
notes.example: Like a busy post room that many senders drop parcels into and many teams collect from, each at their own pace.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Sources for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure Event Hubs?
notes.back: A fully managed, real-time data streaming platform that can ingest millions of events per second with low latency.
notes.explanation: Its built-in Apache Kafka compatibility lets existing Kafka workloads run without code changes or managing clusters.
notes.example: Like a motorway toll plaza with many lanes that takes in huge numbers of vehicles and passes them on, without you running the plaza.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), What is Azure Event Hubs?, “What is Azure Event Hubs?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Azure Event Hubs is a fully managed, real-time data streaming platform that can ingest millions of events per second with low latency. As a native Azure service with built-in Apache Kafka compatibility, Event Hubs enables you to run existing Kafka workloads without code changes or cluster management overhead.

notes.front: What is Azure IoT Hub?
notes.back: A managed service that acts as a central message hub between an IoT application and the devices attached to it.
notes.explanation: It enables reliable and secure communication at scale between the application and its devices.
notes.example: Like a school’s front office that relays messages between the head teacher and hundreds of classrooms, and knows which rooms are allowed to call in.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), What is Azure IoT Hub?, “What is Azure IoT Hub?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Azure IoT Hub is a managed service that acts as a central message hub in a cloud-based IoT solution. It enables reliable and secure communication at scale between an IoT application and its attached devices.

notes.front: What is Azure Stream Analytics?
notes.back: A fully managed stream processing engine that analyses large volumes of streaming data with submillisecond latencies.
notes.explanation: You use it to build streaming pipelines that find patterns and relationships in data from various input sources.
notes.example: Like a hired team of clerks who read every incoming telegram and pass on only the patterns you asked for, while the agency runs the office.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), Welcome to Azure Stream Analytics, “Welcome to Azure Stream Analytics”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Azure Stream Analytics is a fully managed stream processing engine that analyzes and processes large volumes of streaming data with submillisecond latencies. You can build a streaming data pipeline by using Stream Analytics to identify patterns and relationships in data that originates from various input sources

notes.front: What is Spark Structured Streaming?
notes.back: A library built into Apache Spark for working with streaming data as if it were a table that keeps growing.
notes.explanation: It is a good choice when you already use Spark and want to extend that work to real-time data streams.
notes.example: Like a visitors’ book at an open day that keeps gaining signatures, which you can count or summarise at any moment.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore Apache Spark structured streaming, “Spark Structured Streaming”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Spark Structured Streaming, what is a dataframe?
notes.back: A table of rows and columns that Spark reads incoming data into; for a stream, it keeps filling as events arrive.
notes.explanation: Your queries, such as counting events per minute, are written against the dataframe.
notes.example: Like a class register that gains a new line each time a latecomer signs in.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore Apache Spark structured streaming, “Spark Structured Streaming”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric?
notes.back: A Fabric service giving an end-to-end solution for responding to events as they happen, processing flowing data and analysing logs.
notes.explanation: It is meant to let everyone in an organisation extract insights from, and visualise, their data in motion.
notes.example: Like a railway control room where live feeds arrive, are recorded, shown on screens and set off alarms, all in one building.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), What is Real-Time Intelligence?, “What is Real-Time Intelligence?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Real-Time Intelligence is a powerful service that empowers everyone in your organization to extract insights and visualize their data in motion. It offers an end-to-end solution for scenarios where you need to respond to events as they happen, process continuously flowing data, or analyze logs.

notes.front: What is the Real-Time hub in Microsoft Fabric?
notes.back: The central place for all streaming data across an organisation.
notes.explanation: Every Fabric tenant is provisioned with it automatically, with no extra steps to set it up or manage it.
notes.example: Like a station’s departures hall, where every line’s services are listed in one place for anyone to find.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), Introduction to Fabric Real-Time hub, “Introduction to Fabric Real-Time hub”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Real-Time hub is the central place for all streaming data across your entire organization. Every Microsoft Fabric tenant is automatically provisioned with the hub. There are no extra steps needed to set up or manage it.

notes.front: What is an eventstream in Microsoft Fabric?
notes.back: A Real-Time Intelligence feature that brings real-time events into Fabric, transforms them and sends them to destinations, without code.
notes.explanation: You add event sources to the stream, optionally add transformations, and then send the data to supported destinations.
notes.example: Like a sorting conveyor in a parcel depot: parcels come in from several vans, get relabelled, and are pushed down the right chute.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), Overview of Microsoft Fabric eventstreams, “Overview of Microsoft Fabric eventstreams”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Use the eventstreams feature in Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence to bring real-time events into Fabric, transform them, and then send them to various destinations without writing any code. You create an eventstream, add event data sources to the stream, optionally add transformations to transform the event data, and then send the data to supported destinations.

notes.front: What is an eventhouse in Microsoft Fabric?
notes.back: A database designed for storing and analysing streaming data, able to query billions of events in seconds.
notes.explanation: It is built to handle real-time data streams efficiently, so data can be ingested, processed and analysed in near real time.
notes.example: Like a flight recorder that stores every reading from a plane and can be searched instantly, but for a whole business’s events.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), Eventhouse overview, “Eventhouse overview”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Eventhouses are databases designed for storing and analyzing streaming data, so you can query billions of events in seconds. They're designed to handle real-time data streams efficiently, which lets organizations ingest, process, and analyze data in near real-time.

notes.front: In Fabric Real-Time Intelligence, what is a Real-Time Dashboard?
notes.back: A dashboard for live data that anyone can explore through visual tools, natural language and Copilot.
notes.explanation: The training presents it as the Real-Time Intelligence tool for making data in motion easy to understand.
notes.example: Like a station departures board that changes as trains move, rather than a printed timetable pinned to the wall.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence, “Exploring data with real-time intelligence”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Fabric Activator?
notes.back: A no-code event detection engine that automatically triggers actions when specific patterns or conditions are detected in data.
notes.explanation: Its job is to turn data streams into automated actions.
notes.example: Like a smoke alarm wired to call the fire brigade: nobody has to watch it, and it acts the moment its condition is met.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), What is Fabric Activator?, “What is Fabric Activator?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Fabric Activator is a no-code event detection engine that transforms data streams into automated actions. It automatically triggers actions when specific patterns or conditions are detected in data sources.

notes.front: What is Azure Data Explorer?
notes.back: A fully managed, high-performance big data analytics platform for analysing high volumes of data in near real time.
notes.explanation: Its toolbox gives an end-to-end solution covering data ingestion, query, visualisation and management.
notes.example: Like a search engine for a factory’s logbooks that takes in new pages every second and answers questions about them straight away.
notes.source: Azure Data Explorer documentation (MicrosoftDocs/dataexplorer-docs), What is Azure Data Explorer?, “What is Azure Data Explorer?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Azure Data Explorer is a fully managed, high-performance, big data analytics platform that makes it easy to analyze high volumes of data in near real time. The Azure Data Explorer toolbox gives you an end-to-end solution for data ingestion, query, visualization, and management.

notes.front: What are two ways the timing of a batch run can be decided?
notes.back: Any two of: a scheduled interval such as hourly; when a certain amount of data has arrived; another event.
notes.explanation: The training’s everyday example is card billing: one monthly bill covers all of that month’s purchases.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand batch processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two advantages of batch processing?
notes.back: Large volumes are processed efficiently at a convenient time; jobs can run at idle or off-peak times, such as overnight.
notes.explanation: Running jobs in quiet periods improves how well the system’s resources are used.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand batch processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two disadvantages of batch processing?
notes.back: A delay between data input and results; and even small data errors can stop the whole batch job.
notes.explanation: All input must be fully prepared before processing starts, and must be checked carefully before a failed job is rerun.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand batch processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For what kind of operation is stream processing described as ideal?
notes.back: Time-critical operations that need an instant, real-time response.
notes.explanation: Each event is handled when it arrives, with no wait for the next batch interval.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Batch versus stream processing: how do they differ in data scope?
notes.back: Batch can process all the data in the dataset; stream typically sees only the latest data or a rolling time window.
notes.explanation: A rolling window might be, for example, the last 30 seconds of events.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand differences between batch and streaming data”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Batch versus stream processing: what data size is each suited to?
notes.back: Batch: large datasets, handled efficiently. Stream: individual records or micro batches of a few records.
notes.explanation: Data size is one of four differences the training lists, alongside scope, performance and analysis.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand differences between batch and streaming data”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The latency of batch processing is typically {{c1::a few hours}}.
notes.back: a few hours
notes.explanation: Latency here means the time taken for data to be received and processed.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand differences between batch and streaming data”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Stream processing typically happens immediately, with latency in the order of {{c1::seconds or milliseconds}}.
notes.back: seconds or milliseconds
notes.explanation: Performance, measured as latency, is one of the main differences between the two approaches.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand differences between batch and streaming data”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Batch versus stream processing: what kind of analysis is each typically used for?
notes.back: Batch: complex analytics. Stream: simple response functions, aggregates, or calculations such as rolling averages.
notes.explanation: Analysis is one of four differences the training lists, with data scope, data size and performance.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand differences between batch and streaming data”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Even when no real-time analysis is needed, what are streaming technologies often used for?
notes.back: Capturing real-time data and storing it in a data store for later batch processing.
notes.explanation: The training likens this to diverting all the cars on a road into a car park before counting them.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Combine batch and stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a lambda architecture, where does non-streaming data go, and where are the batch results kept?
notes.back: It is ingested into a data store, often a data lake; results go to an analytical store, often a data warehouse.
notes.explanation: Stream processing results may also be persisted in the analytical store to support historical analysis.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Combine batch and stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two platforms does the training give as examples that make kappa-style solutions increasingly practical?
notes.back: Microsoft Fabric and Apache Kafka.
notes.explanation: The training names these as modern platforms suited to treating all data as a continuous stream.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Combine batch and stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the general stream processing architecture, what starts the flow of data?
notes.back: An event that generates some data, such as a sensor signal, a social media post or a log file entry.
notes.explanation: Any occurrence that results in digital data can be such an event.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “A general architecture for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the general stream processing architecture, where is event data captured before processing?
notes.back: In a streaming source: a cloud folder or database table in simple cases, or a queue in more robust solutions.
notes.explanation: A queue can hold logic that makes sure events are processed in order and each event only once.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “A general architecture for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the general stream processing architecture, what three things does the processing stage typically do to event data?
notes.back: Selects data for specific event types, projects data values, and aggregates values over temporal windows.
notes.explanation: This work is often done by a perpetual query, for example counting sensor emissions per minute.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “A general architecture for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why might stream processing results be written to another queue as the sink?
notes.back: So that a subsequent downstream query can process them further.
notes.explanation: Sinks are not always final stores; the output of one query can become the input of the next.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “A general architecture for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Microsoft real-time analytics option is a complete, integrated toolset built into Microsoft Fabric?
notes.back: Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence.
notes.explanation: It bundles eventstreams, eventhouses, Real-Time Dashboards and Activator in one place.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Real-time analytics services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Microsoft real-time analytics option is an open-source library for building streaming solutions on Apache Spark–based services?
notes.back: Spark Structured Streaming.
notes.explanation: It runs on Spark-based services, including Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Real-time analytics services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Microsoft real-time analytics option is a platform as a service for defining streaming jobs?
notes.back: Azure Stream Analytics.
notes.explanation: A job ingests data from a streaming source, applies a perpetual query and writes the results to an output.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Real-time analytics services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the training, for which scenarios is Azure Stream Analytics a solid option?
notes.back: Standalone or hybrid streaming scenarios outside Microsoft Fabric.
notes.explanation: Inside Fabric, the integrated Real-Time Intelligence toolset is the built-in choice.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Real-time analytics services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does data have to flow at high rates and volumes to use Real-Time Intelligence?
notes.back: No. It gives solutions that react to events as they happen, rather than ones that run on a schedule.
notes.explanation: The documentation stresses that “real-time” describes how the solution reacts, not how much data flows.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), What is Real-Time Intelligence?, “Can Real-Time Intelligence help me?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Even though it's called "real-time", your data doesn't have to flow at high rates and volumes. Real-Time Intelligence gives you solutions that react to events as they happen, rather than solutions that run on a schedule.

notes.front: What are two kinds of event processing that eventstreams can perform?
notes.back: Any two of: filtering, data cleansing, transformation, windowed aggregations, duplicate detection.
notes.explanation: This processing lands the data in the shape you want before it reaches its destination.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), What is Real-Time Intelligence?, “Process data streams”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: By using the event processing capabilities in Eventstreams, you can do filtering, data cleansing, transformation, windowed aggregations, and dupe detection, to land the data in the shape you want.

notes.front: What does Fabric create for you automatically when you create an eventstream?
notes.back: An event hub namespace, with an event hub allocated to the default stream.
notes.explanation: Fabric eventstreams are associated with Azure Event Hubs, so no provisioning configuration is needed.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), Overview of Microsoft Fabric eventstreams, “Apache Kafka on Fabric eventstreams”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The Fabric eventstreams feature is associated with Azure Event Hubs, a fully managed cloud-native service. When you create an eventstream, an event hub namespace is automatically created for you. An event hub is allocated to the default stream without requiring any provisioning configurations.

notes.front: What kinds of data are eventhouses tailored to?
notes.back: Time-based, streaming events with structured, semi-structured and unstructured data, such as free text.
notes.explanation: Examples of semi-structured data given are JSON and XML.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), Eventhouse overview, “Eventhouse overview”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Eventhouses are tailored to time-based, streaming events with structured, semistructured (For example, JSON, XML), and unstructured data (For example, free text analysis).

notes.front: How is data in an eventhouse automatically organised for fast searching?
notes.back: By when it arrived.
notes.explanation: This holds even though the data can come from many sources, pipelines and formats.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), Eventhouse overview, “Eventhouse overview”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: and multiple data formats. This data is automatically organized for fast searching based on when it arrived.

notes.front: When does the documentation say to use an eventhouse?
notes.back: For any scenario that includes event-based data, such as telemetry and logs, time series and IoT data, or financial records.
notes.explanation: Security and compliance logs are another example the documentation lists.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), Eventhouse overview, “When do I create an eventhouse?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Use an eventhouse for any scenario that includes event-based data. For example, telemetry and log data, time series and IoT data, security and compliance logs, or financial records.

notes.front: In which two languages can data stored in eventhouses be queried in the KQL queryset?
notes.back: Native KQL (Kusto Query Language) and T-SQL.
notes.explanation: The stored data is indexed and partitioned, ready for fast queries through code, low-code or no-code options.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), What is Real-Time Intelligence?, “Store and analyze data”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The indexed, partitioned data stored in eventhouses is ready for lightning-fast query using various code, low-code, or no-code options in Fabric. Data can be queried in native KQL (Kusto Query Language) or using T-SQL in the KQL queryset.

notes.front: According to the training, what role does the Real-Time hub play in an organisation?
notes.back: A centralised catalogue: one place to discover and share streaming data.
notes.explanation: Sharing streaming data from many sources supports analytics across different teams and domains.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence, “Real-time hub”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two Microsoft services whose streaming data can be ingested into Real-Time hub?
notes.back: Azure Event Hubs and Azure IoT Hub, among others.
notes.explanation: Real-Time hub lists all streaming resources from Microsoft services.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), Introduction to Fabric Real-Time hub, “Data integrations”

notes.evidence: Real-Time hub lists all streaming resources from Microsoft services. Whether it’s Azure Event Hubs, Azure IoT Hub, or other services, you can ingest data into Real-Time hub.

notes.front: With what latency does Activator monitor stateless rules on streaming data?
notes.back: Subsecond.
notes.explanation: It monitors data sources continuously and acts when thresholds are met or patterns are detected.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), What is Fabric Activator?, “What is Fabric Activator?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: It continuously monitors these data sources with low latency (subsecond for stateless rules on streaming data), and initiates actions when thresholds are met or specific patterns are detected.

notes.back: You write a query on the dataframe, and its results are written to a sink.

notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore Apache Spark structured streaming, “Spark Structured Streaming”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: With Spark Structured Streaming, what two roles can the same Delta table play?
notes.back: A streaming sink written in real time, and a source for batch queries.
notes.explanation: So separate storage for historical and live data is not needed.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore Apache Spark structured streaming, “Delta Lake”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What query language does Azure Stream Analytics use?
notes.back: A SQL query language augmented with temporal constraints, for analysing data in motion.
notes.explanation: The temporal constraints are the addition that equips the SQL for data in motion.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), Welcome to Azure Stream Analytics, “Programmer productivity”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Stream Analytics uses a SQL query language that's augmented with powerful temporal constraints to analyze data in motion.

notes.front: Who provisions the hardware and infrastructure for Azure Stream Analytics?
notes.back: Nobody on your side: it is a fully managed PaaS offering, so you provision no hardware or infrastructure.
notes.explanation: Because the job is managed for you, you can focus on business logic rather than infrastructure.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), Welcome to Azure Stream Analytics, “Fully managed service”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Stream Analytics is a fully managed (PaaS) offering on Azure. You don't have to provision any hardware or infrastructure, update OS, or software. Stream Analytics fully manages your job, so you can focus on your business logic and not on the infrastructure.

notes.front: Which two Azure services can a Stream Analytics job connect to for streaming data ingestion?
notes.back: Azure Event Hubs and Azure IoT Hub.

notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: You can create a Stream Analytics job that connects to Azure Event Hubs and Azure IoT Hub for streaming data ingestion, and Azure Blob storage or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 to ingest historical data.

notes.front: What processing and delivery guarantees does Azure Stream Analytics give?
notes.back: Exactly once event processing (with selected outputs) and at-least-once delivery, so events are never lost.

notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), Welcome to Azure Stream Analytics, “Reliability”

notes.evidence: Stream Analytics guarantees exactly once event processing and at-least-once delivery of events, so events are never lost. Exactly once processing is guaranteed with selected output as described in Event Delivery Guarantees.

notes.front: According to the training, how does Azure Event Hubs order and deliver events?
notes.back: Events within a partition are delivered in order, with at-least-once delivery guaranteed.
notes.explanation: The training lists Event Hubs as a service for ingesting high volumes of event data for stream processing.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Sources for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Capture feature of Azure Event Hubs do?
notes.back: Writes streaming data, in near real time, to Azure Blob Storage or Azure Data Lake Storage for long-term retention or batch analytics.
notes.explanation: Capture runs automatically on the same stream used for real-time processing.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), What is Azure Event Hubs?, “Capture”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: your streaming data in near real time to Azure Blob Storage or Azure Data Lake Storage for long-term retention or batch analytics. Capture runs automatically on the same stream used for real-time processing.

notes.front: In which directions can Azure IoT Hub carry information?
notes.back: Both ways: from the device app to cloud services, and from cloud services to the device app.
notes.explanation: Messages are delivered reliably even when the network is interrupted.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), What is Azure IoT Hub?, “Device communication patterns”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: By using IoT Hub, you can send information both from the device app to your cloud services and from your cloud services to the device app. IoT Hub provides reliable messaging and ensures that messages are delivered even in the presence of network interruptions.

notes.front: What must exist in an IoT hub before a device can connect to it?
notes.back: An entry for that device in the hub’s identity registry.
notes.explanation: The device then authenticates using the credentials stored in that registry.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), What is Azure IoT Hub?, “Connect and authenticate devices”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Before a device or module can connect, the IoT hub's identity registry must have an entry for that device or module. A device or module authenticates with the IoT hub based on credentials stored in the identity registry.

notes.front: Which storage service does the training list as a possible streaming source, although it is more often used for batch processing?
notes.back: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2.
notes.explanation: The training describes it as a highly scalable storage service.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Sources for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When Azure Event Hubs is used as a sink, what is it for?
notes.back: Queuing the processed data for further downstream processing.
notes.explanation: The same service can therefore sit at either end of a streaming pipeline.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Sinks for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which sinks does the training name for persisting processed stream results as files?
notes.back: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, OneLake, or Azure Blob Storage.
notes.explanation: These are file stores, as opposed to the table-based sinks used for querying.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Sinks for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which sinks does the training name for persisting processed stream results in a table for querying and analysis?
notes.back: Azure SQL Database, Azure Databricks, or Microsoft Fabric.
notes.explanation: The training sets these table sinks apart from the file sinks used simply to persist results.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Sinks for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which query language do you use to query Azure Data Explorer?
notes.back: Kusto Query Language (KQL), an open-source language created by the Azure Data Explorer team.
notes.explanation: It is described as simple to learn, with both simple operators and advanced analytics; T-SQL is also supported.
notes.source: Azure Data Explorer documentation (MicrosoftDocs/dataexplorer-docs), What is Azure Data Explorer?, “User-friendly query language”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Query Azure Data Explorer by using Kusto Query Language (KQL), an open-source language that the Azure Data Explorer team created. The language is simple to understand and learn, and highly productive. You can use simple operators and advanced analytics. Azure Data Explorer also supports T-SQL.

notes.front: According to its documentation, what is Azure Data Explorer ideal for?
notes.back: Interactive analytics over high-velocity, diverse raw data.
notes.explanation: Its documentation also offers a decision tree to help you judge whether it is right for your case.
notes.source: Azure Data Explorer documentation (MicrosoftDocs/dataexplorer-docs), What is Azure Data Explorer?, “When should you use Azure Data Explorer?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Azure Data Explorer is ideal for enabling interactive analytics capabilities over high-velocity, diverse raw data. Use the following decision tree to help you decide if Azure Data Explorer is right for you:

notes.front: How much data can Azure Data Explorer query, and how quickly are results returned?
notes.back: Petabytes, with results returned within milliseconds to seconds.
notes.explanation: It can also ingest terabytes of data in minutes through queued or streaming ingestion.
notes.source: Azure Data Explorer documentation (MicrosoftDocs/dataexplorer-docs), What is Azure Data Explorer?, “Data velocity, variety, and volume”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: With Azure Data Explorer, you can ingest terabytes of data in minutes via queued ingestion or streaming ingestion. You can query petabytes of data, with results returned within milliseconds to seconds.

notes.front: Can a Kusto query write data?
notes.back: No. A Kusto query is a read-only request to process data and return results.
notes.explanation: The request is stated in plain text, using a data-flow model that is easy to read, author and automate.
notes.source: Azure Data Explorer documentation (MicrosoftDocs/dataexplorer-docs), Kusto Query Language overview, “What is a Kusto query?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A Kusto query is a read-only request to process data and return results. The request is stated in plain text, using a data-flow model that is easy to read, author, and automate.

notes.front: A water company reads meters all quarter and sends each household one bill covering the whole period. Is that batch or stream processing?
notes.back: Batch processing.
notes.explanation: The readings are collected and stored, then processed together as one group at the end of the period.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand batch processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A chemical plant must close a valve within a second of any pressure reading going over a limit. Is that batch or stream processing?
notes.back: Stream processing.
notes.explanation: It is a time-critical operation that needs an instant response to each new reading, which is what stream processing is for.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A web team wants a rolling average of page views over the last minute, updated continuously. Which approach fits, with what typical latency?
notes.back: B: stream processing, with latency of seconds or milliseconds.
notes.choices:
A) Batch processing, with latency of a few hours
B) Stream processing, with latency of seconds or milliseconds
C) Batch processing, with latency of milliseconds
D) Stream processing, with latency of a few hours
notes.choicesExplained: A: batch results typically arrive hours later, too late for a live figure. C: batch latency is typically hours, not milliseconds. D: stream processing typically happens immediately, not hours later.
notes.explanation: Rolling averages over recent data are exactly the simple calculations stream processing is used for.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand differences between batch and streaming data”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A city council wants a live dashboard of cyclists passing counters, plus year-on-year analysis that combines the live results with nightly-processed survey data. Which pattern fits?
notes.back: D: lambda architecture.
notes.choices:
A) Kappa architecture with no data store
B) Batch processing only, run weekly
C) A single perpetual query with no sink
D) Lambda architecture
notes.choicesExplained: A: kappa drops the batch layer, but the council has batch-processed survey data to combine. B: weekly batches cannot drive a live dashboard. C: without a sink, nothing is kept for year-on-year analysis.
notes.explanation: Lambda captures streaming data for real-time views while batch processing other sources, and both results can be kept in an analytical store.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Combine batch and stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which order matches the general stream processing architecture?
notes.back: D: event, streaming source, processing, sink.
notes.choices:
A) Sink, processing, streaming source, event
B) Streaming source, sink, event, processing
C) Processing, event, sink, streaming source
D) Event, streaming source, processing, sink
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and A: data must first be generated by an event and captured in a source before it can be processed, and results are written to the sink last.
notes.explanation: An event generates data, the source captures it, a query processes it, and the results are written to an output.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “A general architecture for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A stadium wants the number of turnstile entries in every five-minute period, from a live feed. What does the processing stage use?
notes.back: D: a perpetual query aggregating over a temporal window.
notes.choices:
A) A one-off query run after the match
B) A nightly batch job over the day’s files
C) A dataframe written straight to a sink with no query
D) A perpetual query that aggregates over a temporal window
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: both wait until data is at rest, so no live five-minute counts. C: without a query, nothing counts the entries.
notes.explanation: Counting events per fixed time period is aggregation over a temporal window, and a perpetual query keeps doing it as data arrives.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “A general architecture for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A streaming job’s processed results must be kept as files for later historical analysis. Which is a suitable sink?
notes.back: A: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2
B) Azure IoT Hub
C) A temporal window
D) Apache Kafka acting as the source
notes.choicesExplained: B: IoT Hub ingests data from devices; it is a source, not a file store. C: a window is a period for aggregation, not an output. D: a source feeds the processing; it does not persist results.
notes.explanation: The training lists Data Lake Storage Gen2, OneLake and Blob Storage as sinks for persisting results as files.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Sinks for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A data team already runs Spark notebooks in Azure Databricks for batch work and wants to extend the same code base to real-time streams. Which option fits best?
notes.back: D: Spark Structured Streaming.
notes.choices:
A) Azure IoT Hub
B) Azure Data Explorer
C) A Real-Time Dashboard
D) Spark Structured Streaming
notes.choicesExplained: A: IoT Hub ingests device data but does not run Spark code. B: Data Explorer is a separate analytics platform queried with KQL. C: a dashboard visualises data; it does not process it.
notes.explanation: Spark Structured Streaming is the option for teams already using Spark who want to add real-time streams.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore Apache Spark structured streaming, “Spark Structured Streaming”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A retailer’s analytics already live in Microsoft Fabric. It wants to ingest till events, store and query them, show live charts and send alerts, all in one integrated toolset. What should it use?
notes.back: C: Fabric Real-Time Intelligence.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Stream Analytics
B) Batch processing in a data warehouse
C) Fabric Real-Time Intelligence
D) Azure IoT Hub alone
notes.choicesExplained: A: Stream Analytics suits standalone or hybrid scenarios outside Fabric. B: batch results come hours later, so no live charts or instant alerts. D: IoT Hub only ingests data; it does not store, chart or alert.
notes.explanation: Real-Time Intelligence is the complete, integrated real-time toolset built into Fabric, covering ingestion, storage, dashboards and actions.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Real-time analytics services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A logistics firm does not use Fabric. It wants a managed service where it writes a SQL-like query that averages lorry speeds every minute and writes the results to Azure SQL Database. Which fits?
notes.back: D: Azure Stream Analytics.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2
B) Fabric Activator
C) Apache Kafka
D) Azure Stream Analytics
notes.choicesExplained: A: a storage service, not a query engine. B: Activator triggers actions and belongs to Fabric, which the firm does not use. C: Kafka ingests data; it is not the managed query service described.
notes.explanation: Its SQL query language is augmented with temporal constraints for analysing data in motion.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), Welcome to Azure Stream Analytics, “Programmer productivity”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Stream Analytics uses a SQL query language that's augmented with powerful temporal constraints to analyze data in motion.

notes.front: An energy firm has thousands of smart thermostats. It must ingest their readings and also send configuration commands back to individual devices. Which ingestion service fits best?
notes.back: B: Azure IoT Hub.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2
B) Azure IoT Hub
C) A Real-Time Dashboard
D) Azure Data Explorer
notes.choicesExplained: A: a storage service, not a two-way device hub. C: a dashboard visualises data but ingests nothing from devices. D: an analytics platform, not a device messaging hub.
notes.explanation: IoT Hub carries information from cloud services to the device app as well as from devices to the cloud.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), What is Azure IoT Hub?, “Device communication patterns”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: By using IoT Hub, you can send information both from the device app to your cloud services and from your cloud services to the device app.

notes.front: A shopping website produces millions of click events a minute from applications that already publish with Kafka clients. The team wants a managed ingestion service without changing that code. Which fits?
notes.back: D: Azure Event Hubs.
notes.choices:
A) Azure IoT Hub
B) Azure SQL Database
C) Fabric Activator
D) Azure Event Hubs
notes.choicesExplained: A: IoT Hub is optimised for IoT devices, not web applications. B: a relational database, not a high-volume event ingestion service. C: Activator triggers actions; it does not ingest the stream.
notes.explanation: Event Hubs ingests millions of events per second and runs existing Kafka workloads without code changes.
notes.source: Azure documentation (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs), What is Azure Event Hubs?, “What is Azure Event Hubs?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Azure Event Hubs is a fully managed, real-time data streaming platform that can ingest millions of events per second with low latency. As a native Azure service with built-in Apache Kafka compatibility, Event Hubs enables you to run existing Kafka workloads without code changes or cluster management overhead.

notes.front: In Fabric, a team needs to store months of application logs as they stream in and query billions of events in seconds with KQL. Which item should hold the data?
notes.back: B: an eventhouse.
notes.choices:
A) An eventstream
B) An eventhouse
C) Activator
D) The Real-Time hub
notes.choicesExplained: A: an eventstream ingests, transforms and routes events; it is not the store. C: Activator triggers actions on conditions. D: the hub is a catalogue for discovering streaming data, not a database.
notes.explanation: Log data is one of the event-based scenarios for which the documentation recommends an eventhouse.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), Eventhouse overview, “When do I create an eventhouse?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Use an eventhouse for any scenario that includes event-based data. For example, telemetry and log data, time series and IoT data, security and compliance logs, or financial records.

notes.front: A food bank streams freezer temperatures into Fabric. It wants an email sent to the duty manager whenever any freezer rises above −15 °C. Which Fabric item should do this?
notes.back: D: Activator.
notes.choices:
A) An eventhouse
B) A Real-Time Dashboard
C) The Real-Time hub
D) Activator
notes.choicesExplained: A: an eventhouse stores and queries data but does not send the email itself. B: a dashboard shows the data to people who are looking at it. C: the hub is for discovering and sharing streams.
notes.explanation: Sending emails is among the actions Activator can take.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation (MicrosoftDocs/fabric-docs), What is Fabric Activator?, “What is Fabric Activator?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: These actions can include sending emails or Teams notifications, launching Power Automate flows, or integrating with third-party systems.

notes.front: A new analyst wants to find out which streaming data sources already exist across her organisation’s Fabric tenant and which she can use. Where should she look?
notes.back: A: the Real-Time hub.
notes.choices:
A) The Real-Time hub
B) A KQL query against one eventhouse
C) An Activator rule
D) A Spark dataframe
notes.choicesExplained: B: one eventhouse shows only its own data. C: a rule reacts to data; it does not list sources. D: a dataframe holds data being processed, not an organisation-wide list.
notes.explanation: The Real-Time hub is the single, tenant-wide place to discover and share streaming data.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence, “Real-time hub”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team wants to bring delivery-van events into Fabric, drop test messages, and route the rest to an eventhouse, without writing code. What should it create?
notes.back: A: an eventstream.
notes.choices:
A) An eventstream
B) A Kusto query
C) A Real-Time Dashboard
D) An Azure Data Explorer cluster
notes.choicesExplained: C: a dashboard visualises data but does not route it. B: a Kusto query is read-only and returns results; it does not route events. D: a separate service outside Fabric, and not a no-code router.
notes.explanation: Eventstreams bring events into Fabric, filter and transform them, and send them to destinations without code.

notes.front: An operator outside Fabric wants interactive, ad hoc analysis of raw, fast-arriving telemetry that has not been curated, using KQL. Which Azure service fits?
notes.back: B: Azure Data Explorer.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Event Hubs
B) Azure Data Explorer
C) Azure Stream Analytics
D) Azure Blob Storage
notes.choicesExplained: A: Event Hubs ingests events but is not an interactive analytics platform. C: Stream Analytics runs continuous SQL jobs, not ad hoc KQL analysis. D: a storage service with no query engine.
notes.explanation: Data Explorer is ideal for interactive analytics over high-velocity, diverse raw data.
notes.source: Azure Data Explorer documentation (MicrosoftDocs/dataexplorer-docs), What is Azure Data Explorer?, “When should you use Azure Data Explorer?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Azure Data Explorer is ideal for enabling interactive analytics capabilities over high-velocity, diverse raw data.

notes.front: Batch versus stream processing: when is each new data record processed?
notes.back: Batch: with its group, when the batch runs. Stream: as soon as it arrives.
notes.explanation: Batch waits for a schedule, a data threshold or another event; stream processing has no batch interval to wait for.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Understand batch and stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Lambda versus kappa architecture: how do they handle batch work?
notes.back: Lambda combines a batch layer with stream processing; kappa has no separate batch layer and replays the stream instead.
notes.explanation: Kappa is presented as the simpler alternative because it treats all data as a continuous stream.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Understand batch and stream processing, “Combine batch and stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Azure IoT Hub versus Azure Event Hubs: how does the training distinguish them?
notes.back: Both ingest event data; IoT Hub is optimised to manage event data from Internet-of-things devices.
notes.explanation: Event Hubs is the general service for ingesting high volumes of event data from any producer.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Sources for stream processing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Azure Stream Analytics versus Fabric Real-Time Intelligence: where does each sit?
notes.back: Stream Analytics is a standalone Azure PaaS service; Real-Time Intelligence is a toolset built into Microsoft Fabric.
notes.explanation: That is why the training points to Stream Analytics for scenarios outside Fabric.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Real-time analytics services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Eventstream versus eventhouse: what does each do in Real-Time Intelligence?
notes.back: An eventstream ingests, routes and transforms streaming data; an eventhouse is a database for storing and querying it.
notes.explanation: Data typically flows through an eventstream and lands in an eventhouse, where it is queried with KQL.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, Explore common elements of stream processing architecture, “Real-time analytics services”
